findings.title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
findings.body: `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, which subclass `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, *not* `multiprocessing.context.Process` (what `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is always False and `kill()` is never executed. Consequences: (a) a process detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`, i.e. it is still alive but has not updated `healthy_since`) is left running while a replacement process is spawned for the *same* shards — two flushers then flush/produce the same shard set, risking duplicate and/or fragmented segments on `buffered-segments`; (b) dead processes are never reaped (no `kill`/`join`/`close`), leaving zombies; (c) the same broken check at line 346 in `join()` means `terminate()` is never called on shutdown. The intent was clearly to distinguish processes from threads — use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`).

findings.title: No validation of flusher process count; 0/negative values silently disable flushing
findings.body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` followed by `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` has two bad edge cases reachable from the new `--flusher-processes` CLI option: passing `0` falls through the `or` and silently means "one process per shard" (the opposite of what the help text 'Maximum number of processes ... Defaults to 1' implies), and passing a negative number yields `num_processes <= 0`, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and **no flusher process is started at all**. In that case spans keep being written to Redis but no segments are ever flushed or produced, until Redis memory backpressure stalls the consumer. The same happens if `assigned_shards` is empty. Validate the option (require >= 1) and/or clamp `num_processes` to at least 1.

findings.title: Metric tag contains the comma-joined list of all shards, causing high-cardinality tags (and a tag key typo)
findings.body: `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` is used as the value of the `shard` tag on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (emitted per segment) and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. With the default `--flusher-processes 1`, a single process owns all assigned shards, so the tag value becomes e.g. `"0,1,2,...,63"` and differs per pod/partition assignment, producing a distinct time series per consumer instance — a cardinality explosion on a per-segment distribution metric, and it makes the previously untagged `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` unusable for simple aggregation. Additionally line 199 uses the tag key `shards` while lines 185/192 use `shard`, so the three metrics are not tagged consistently. Prefer emitting per-shard tags (or no shard tag) with a stable, low-cardinality value.

findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces the attribute on the `time` module itself. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62, with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change', therefore does nothing at all. The test still depends on the flusher thread happening to flush before `step.join()` sets the stop flag, i.e. it is racy, and the comment misleads future readers into thinking a wait was added. Either don't patch `time.sleep` globally (e.g. patch it only in the flusher module) or wait on an actual condition (poll until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout).

findings.title: New multi-process flusher test only asserts internal bookkeeping, not that all shards are flushed
findings.body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and `sum(len(shards)) == 4`, then immediately joins without submitting any spans. It never verifies the behaviour the PR introduces: that spans landing on each of the 4 shards are actually flushed and produced by the two flusher workers, and that shards are partitioned without overlap (the `sum == 4` assertion would also pass for a duplicated mapping such as `{0: [0, 0], 1: [1, 1]}`, which would cause double-production). It also exercises only the thread path (`produce_to_pipe` is set), so the real spawn-process path with multiple workers remains untested. Add a test that writes spans for several shards, advances the drift, and asserts every segment is produced exactly once, plus an assertion that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals `assigned_shards` with no duplicates.

findings.title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` in `_ensure_processes_alive`). Leaving it in place is confusing — it suggests per-shard restart is supported, and if someone later calls it, it restarts the whole process group for the shard without resetting the restart counter bookkeeping that `_ensure_processes_alive` relies on. Remove it.

findings.title: A new parent-side SpansBuffer (and Redis client) is created on every process restart and never released
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shards` constructs `shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing the previous instance without closing it. Each restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per worker) therefore leaks the Redis client/connection pool of the discarded buffer in the consumer process. In addition, the parent now holds one buffer per worker group on top of the buffer passed in from the factory, so `submit()` performs N `record_stored_segments()`/`get_memory_info()` round trips per call instead of one. Consider reusing a single parent-side buffer for stats/memory checks and only creating per-shard buffers for the children.
